definition: Based on whim or an insufficiently justified choice rather than a clear reason.
example: The policy imposed an arbitrary fee unrelated to the cost of the service.
nuance: Arbitrary need not mean statistically random; a deliberate decision can still lack justification.
prompt: A rule sets different limits without explaining why the difference matters.
options: The arbitrary cutoff excluded similar cases without a relevant justification.
The arbitrary cutoff followed directly from a carefully validated safety threshold.
The cutoff was arbitrary because everyone agreed on its well-supported rationale.
The arbitrary cutoff was set by a neutral panel after hearing evidence from both sides.
reasons: This sentence demonstrates the meaning: based on whim or an insufficiently justified choice rather than a clear reason.
A validated relevant reason makes the cutoff justified rather than arbitrary.
Agreement alone is not enough, but a well-supported rationale contradicts the intended meaning.
This confuses the word with arbitration; a ruling made by weighing both sides' evidence is reasoned, not arbitrary.

practice.prompt: A coach announces which players will start in Saturday's game.
options: The lineup seemed arbitrary because every starter had posted the highest scores in the week's practice drills.
The arbitrary official stood at midfield and settled a dispute between the two captains.
The coach made attendance arbitrary, so players could skip practice whenever they liked.
The lineup felt arbitrary because the coach ignored practice stats and picked starters on a hunch.
reasons: Choices tied directly to recorded performance have a clear reason, so they are the opposite of arbitrary.
This confuses the word with arbiter; it describes unjustified choices, not someone who settles disputes.
The word describes how a decision was made, not whether something is optional.
Picking starters on impulse while ignoring the relevant evidence leaves the choice without a real basis.
